name: Logical Clocks
intent: Order events in a distributed system by cause and effect instead of by wall-clock time, using counters that travel with messages, because physical clocks on different machines never agree exactly.
scenario: A chat service sorts messages by the timestamp of the sender's phone. Alice's phone clock is 5 seconds fast, so her question appears after Bob's reply. Nothing is wrong with the code. The clocks simply disagree.
problem: Each machine has its own clock, and they drift and are adjusted by different amounts. Network delays make it impossible to compare timestamps exactly. Yet systems need to know which of two events came first, or whether neither influenced the other. Using physical time gives wrong answers, and sometimes silently loses writes (last write wins by clock).

howItWorks.title: What matters is 'happened before'
howItWorks.text: Event A happened before event B if A could have influenced B: they are on the same machine with A earlier, or A is the sending of a message that B receives, or there is a chain of such steps. If neither can reach the other, the events are concurrent: no order between them is meaningful.

howItWorks.title: Lamport clocks: a counter that obeys causality
howItWorks.text: Each process keeps a number. It increments it before every event, stamps outgoing messages with it, and on receiving a message sets its counter to the maximum of its own and the message's, plus one. If A happened before B then A's number is smaller than B's. So sorting by Lamport time never puts an effect before its cause.

howItWorks.title: The limit of Lamport clocks
howItWorks.text: A smaller number does not prove 'happened before': two unrelated events can have any ordering of numbers. Lamport time gives a consistent order, but it cannot tell you whether two events were concurrent.

howItWorks.title: Vector clocks detect concurrency
howItWorks.text: Each process keeps a vector with one counter per process. Comparing two vectors tells you exactly one of three things: A happened before B (every entry less than or equal, and one smaller), B before A, or they are concurrent (each is ahead somewhere). Databases use this to notice conflicting concurrent writes and keep both for the application to merge.

howItWorks.title: Hybrid and bounded physical clocks
howItWorks.text: Hybrid logical clocks combine a physical timestamp with a counter, giving readable times that still respect causality. Google's Spanner uses very accurate clocks with a known error bound and waits out the uncertainty. Whatever you choose, never rely on raw wall-clock comparison between machines to decide who wrote last.

pros: Correct ordering of causally related events regardless of clock skew
Vector clocks reveal true concurrency and conflicts
No clock synchronisation hardware or trust in clocks is needed
Cheap: a counter or a small vector attached to messages
cons: Vector clocks grow with the number of participants
Logical time has no relation to real time, so it cannot say 'within the last hour'
Every message and every stored item must carry the metadata
whenToUse: Ordering events or messages across machines (chat, logs, collaboration)
Detecting conflicting concurrent updates in replicated stores
Anywhere 'last write wins by timestamp' could silently lose data
whenNotToUse: A single machine or single leader that can assign sequence numbers itself
When a consensus system already gives you a total order
pitfalls: Using System.currentTimeMillis or DateTime.Now from different servers to decide the newest value
Assuming NTP-synchronised clocks are close enough to be compared exactly
Vectors that grow without bound as clients come and go
Treating a Lamport timestamp as proof that one event caused another
